rubric:
[STAGE-EVIDENCE] Rule: Check that the agent used the requested, loaded skill on the actual service and stayed within that role's permissions.
Example: An audit may say that worker context is missing and propose a test. It must not describe that planned test as a successful run.
Evidence: Audit and verification are read-only. An audit describes missing SDKs, exporters or application-owned propagation as source gaps and future checks, not work already executed. Advice to delegate is optional: do not require another model or a statement that the agent understood the instructions. An audit plan is not proof of an executed baseline. Judge missing required execution under EXECUTED-COMPLETION and the standalone missing-prerequisite case under PREREQUISITE-NEGATIVE; that exception never applies to a paired positive workflow. Judge an item's incorrectly derived status under DERIVED-STATUS, without failing this item for that same status error. Any verification edit, including in a genuine missing-prerequisite case, fails this item.
Insufficient evidence: A plan described as executed work, or verification that edits the supplied application.

[EXECUTED-COMPLETION] Rule: For instrumentation, make the planned changes, start the real application, run the project's checks and normal verification, and pass the host checker without changing it.
Example: A report can honestly say verification was not run. That disclosure does not satisfy a task that requires completed instrumentation and verification.
Evidence: Scope and required checks: Instrumentation must implement the approved or default baseline, start the real application, run project checks and normal verification, and pass the unchanged host checker. A plan, Not run result, validated report saying nothing ran, or receipt-gate N_A does not meet this requirement. Ordinary pytest does not waive the instrumentation checker: missing required evidence is not_proven, even if the agent claims success. Verification must actually run its required read-only checks on the supplied instrumented workspace. The paired runner's extra checker run proves only the facts identified in its current execution context; this item does not require every verification task to run a host checker. Audit and a genuine untouched standalone missing-prerequisite verification case are not applicable here and receive no runtime credit. This item checks required execution; BAKED-EVIDENCE separately checks the required bake, receipt and validation provenance.
Insufficient evidence: An agent success statement, a plan, or a receipt saying no execution occurred in place of required execution.

[PREREQUISITE-NEGATIVE] Rule: Use this exception only when a standalone verification task starts from an untouched fixture that is missing a required audit or selection.
Example: A standalone verification fixture with no required audit may stop after confirming that blocker. An already instrumented paired workflow may not use that exception.
Evidence: First inspect and confirm those missing prerequisites. The agent may then report the exact blocker, without editing files, inventing reports or claiming runtime success. Checks that require proceeding beyond that blocker are not_applicable, with the reason 'prerequisite-negative'; they receive no runtime credit and need no post-gate analysis. This item itself is not applicable to other tasks, including the paired instrumented workflow. Decide applicability from the supplied starting fixture; later agent edits cannot change the task into this exception. A false exception claim cannot waive STAGE-EVIDENCE or EXECUTED-COMPLETION. Judge a verification edit under STAGE-EVIDENCE and cite it here without failing both items for that same edit.
Insufficient evidence: A claimed prerequisite blocker without inspecting the actual starting fixture, or using this exception for a paired positive workflow.

[CANONICAL-BINDINGS] Rule: Preserve the established audit and selection hashes, IDs, source bindings and role permissions.
Example: Verification must not delete a selected requirement from the audit just because its test is difficult to pass.
Evidence: Verification must not edit the audit or change what it is bound to. Instrumentation must stay within the approved work. Do not remove an established, critical or operator requirement to avoid testing it. A direct workflow without an audit must use its actual plan, results and source evidence; it must not invent canonical audit, selection or verification JSON.
Insufficient evidence: A rewritten audit or withdrawn requirement used to avoid the selected work.

[SELECTED-CONTRACT] Rule: Before finalizing new audit IDs or a direct plan, read every saved requirement that affects the work.
Example: If a scenario refers to shared retry parameters, read that shared block before planning the check; the scenario row alone is not the full requirement.
Evidence: Scope and required checks: Before finalizing new audit IDs or a direct plan, read all saved requirements relevant to the work: proposed fixes, acceptance and shared constraints, telemetry fields, scenario triggers and outcomes, environments, imported test cases, required event order, and source or operator promises. Follow references and read relevant fields omitted from a projection. 'required-controls --view contracts', or an equally complete inspection, can expose this material; the default telemetry hints are not a complete inventory. Completed, manual or externally owned prerequisites are context to inspect, not permission to execute them, proof they can run, or proof of completion. Retrieve any required source sections cut off by tool output. This item checks input inspection and inventory. Judge a wholly missing promised branch under CLAIM-COMPLETENESS; fail this item only when there is separate evidence of a missing input or inspection.
Insufficient evidence: Reading only a projected row while omitting relevant saved constraints or referenced cases.

[ADDRESSABLE-ORACLES] Rule: For every required variant and outcome, identify its test input, a specific assertion and a place where the outcome can actually be observed.
Example: A test that eventually receives one log cannot distinguish a nonblocking handler from one that blocked first and then succeeded.
Evidence: Keep any conditions on when that case applies. Shared or grouped tests are valid when every member's inputs, expected result and required independent observation are explicit; do not require duplicate tests, repeated prose or particular case names. An implied property counts only if breaking it would fail that same test path in the relevant phase. For example, eventual success does not prove that work was nonblocking. A heading, case label or field mention is not an assertion. Judge a present assertion that cannot detect its claimed failure here; judge a wholly omitted promised branch under CLAIM-COMPLETENESS. Neither verdict automatically determines the other. When an assertion lets another operation's observation satisfy its control, judge that selector under OPERATION-COVERAGE. Do not also fail this item for the same predicate unless a separate detection weakness is evidenced.
Insufficient evidence: A label or eventual success that cannot detect the specific failure being tested.

[SAVED-READBACK] Rule: After the last edit that changes a promise, read the saved requirements and check that the final expectations agree, including shared constraints and referenced test cases.
Example: If the final plan adds a second shutdown signal, read the saved plan again and reconcile its expected result before finalizing.
Evidence: Generating a projection without reading it does not count. Audit must do this saved-output check without executing the application. If delegated findings are used, the parent must verify the concrete findings within its existing authority and rerun affected checks or retain the gap. Delegation advice is not evidence of execution or approval, and no extra model is required. This item checks final saved-output agreement, required readback and verification of delegated findings. A missing promised check belongs to CLAIM-COMPLETENESS; report a separate mismatch or missing readback here only with its own evidence.
Insufficient evidence: Generating a saved projection without reading it, or relying on expectations from before the last promise-changing edit.

[EXECUTION-FRESHNESS] Rule: After the last relevant code, test or configuration change, rerun the affected checks and read their new final outputs.
Example: Two trials using the same case may have identical input values, but their actual workspaces and evidence must not accidentally alias.
Evidence: Bind the evidence to the current source, dependencies, commands, actual case inputs and outcome counts, and retain failures. Use required project runtimes and configured local endpoints. A copied receipt or an exit code of zero without execution does not prove the current run. Identify the actual storage and inputs for each trial. Separate trials must not accidentally share evidence files; paths differing only in letter case can refer to the same file. Separate harness folders alone do not prove separate agent evidence. This item checks freshness, final rerun/readback and actual trial/input identity; do not fail it solely because another item lacks a promised control.
Insufficient evidence: Old results, unread regenerated outputs, or separate harness folders that actually refer to the same agent evidence.

[DERIVED-STATUS] Rule: Set each control's or item's status and related report fields only from its own assertions and raw results.
Example: If three required controls have passing observations and the fourth has none, keep the fourth Not proven rather than copying the group's success to it.
Evidence: Scope and required checks: Derive each control or item's status, direct-assertion flag, proof mode, visibility, trace IDs and remaining work from its own assertions and raw results. Required controls without matching proof remain Not proven. Related passes, copied acceptance results or unconditional success assignments cannot close them. Attribute IDs only to the operation and phase that produced them. A valid unsampled context-only observation may retain its own IDs; an outside-context observation has none; unknown ownership stays unresolved. A direct item assertion may pass while supporting scenarios remain incomplete, provided the item's stated scope is still accurate.
Insufficient evidence: A summary that assigns success without a matching assertion and raw result for that item.

[CONFIG-SCOPE] Rule: Check the application's own settings and any overrides we add, the supplied settings that affect this work, the inputs needed to keep application or operator requirements, and every capability or default the work claims.
Example: A versioned SDK default can be documented from source. A newly added application override needs its own ownership and behavior checked.
Evidence: An unchanged default delegated to a named SDK version is a source fact, not a promise to test every upstream input at runtime. State who owns each setting, its default, and any unsupported or unverified behavior. Do not invent tests for unused SDK combinations. Delegation must not excuse ignored active inputs, an incorrect exact claim or an unresolved critical application requirement.
Insufficient evidence: Calling an active application override an SDK default, or using delegation to dismiss a required unresolved guarantee.

[CONFIG-READER] Rule: For each required setting, find the code that actually reads it and follow the value to where it is used.
Example: An environment option may be declared publicly yet never reach the provider constructed by application startup.
Evidence: Scope and required checks: For each required setting, identify the actual public option or operator/environment reader and follow the value to where it is used. Inspect the relevant conversion, precedence, special default values, units, validation, clamps, merge or detector order, and diagnostic helpers. Distinguish native API values from serialized values and keep different owners and defaults separate. If the SDK already reads the environment, do not require a new application parser. An option declaration or unused helper does not prove startup uses it. For a selected Go detector collision, test preservation through that same Resource initialization. This item checks readers, precedence and final use; NORMAL-LAUNCH separately checks preservation through the actual launcher. A helper-only test does not prove launcher behavior, and missing launcher proof alone does not prove a reader bug.
Insufficient evidence: An option declaration, unused helper, or service-name-only probe that does not establish the selected reader and precedence.

[CONFIG-INPUTS] Rule: Test the kinds of input that reach the reader in question, or that an exact claim depends on.
Example: If startup replaces an invalid timeout with a default, test both the invalid input and the value actually consumed after fallback.
Evidence: Scope and required checks: Test the input classes that reach the relevant reader or support an exact claim: applicable letter casing, empty and absent values, invalid values, numbers, fractions, range limits, overflow, enum or no-op values, fallbacks and higher-priority inputs. Use assertions that distinguish the promised accepted value, rejection or diagnostic through the actual caller, including its fallback values. Valid typed options used only to set up a test need proof of the applied value, units, real reader and intended startup state; they do not require an unrelated parser suite. Removing a parent environment key proves absence only if startup or child overrides do not restore it. This item checks reader/parser inputs. Judge normal-launch Resource identity profiles under NORMAL-LAUNCH, without failing both items for the same missing launch.
Insufficient evidence: Inspecting environment text without exercising the relevant caller, fallback and input classes.

[SIGNAL-ACTIVATION] Rule: For each signal, cover every selected or promised exporter and every way it can be turned on or off, including each reachable branch.
Example: Disabling log export does not show that an explicit metrics opt-out is respected.
Evidence: Scope and required checks: Cover each selected or promised exporter and activation mode for each signal, including reachable absent, empty, none, other-exporter and protocol branches. Distinguish disabling the whole SDK from disabling logs, preserving propagation, or changing a bridge flag. A logs-only opt-out does not prove trace or metric settings. A selected non-OTLP branch must preserve native output and add no local OTLP pipeline; do not install an exporter the operator did not select. Keep supported and rejected transport outcomes consistent with the plan and the actual owner's normalization rules, including supported Python mixed lists. This item checks activation branches and whether they invoke required policy checks. LOCAL-DESTINATION checks receiver approval/resolution; CREDENTIAL-ISOLATION checks header preservation. One missing policy fact must not automatically fail all three.
Insufficient evidence: Using a logs-only opt-out to claim trace/metric opt-out coverage, or bypassing required policy on another selected exporter branch.

[PROOF-BOUNDARY] Rule: Label each result with the proof mode that matches the path the test actually exercised.
Example: A direct SDK emit decoded at loopback can prove unit+otlp, but it does not show that the application's normal logger and launcher work.
Evidence: Scope and required checks: Assign proof modes from the path actually asserted: an isolated SDK/bridge unit test; unit+otlp with decoded loopback SDK output; app_test using actual application setup or helpers; or full_runtime through the claimed normal application path. An audit's proof_level describes a planned focused call-site check, full-runtime check or justified choice of either; it is not an execution mode. 'Either' needs adequate alternatives for the same requirement. Each proof mode and visibility value must accurately cover all parts of its assertion and any requirement to prove them on the same path. Do not borrow another probe's stronger proof mode. Do not downgrade a direct runtime item solely because supporting scenarios are focused or incomplete. Optional modes need their actual source-supported names, units, fields and aliases; a test for the default mode cannot prove them without qualification.
Insufficient evidence: Borrowing a stronger proof mode from a different probe or treating a synthetic SDK test as normal application execution.

[NORMAL-LAUNCH] Rule: Plan or test the selected Resource identity cases by starting the application through its real launcher.
Example: Deleting OTEL_SERVICE_NAME in the parent process does not establish Resource-only startup if the active profile adds it back.
Evidence: Scope and required checks: Plan or test the selected Resource identity cases through the real launcher: service.name supplied only through Resource attributes, a supported explicit override, and fully absent identity when selected. Fallbacks must preserve SDK-parsed operator identity, supported encoding and whitespace, and unrelated attributes. Build the actual child environment, removing conflicting inherited keys and accounting for loaders or profiles. Promised service.version or other fields need their own expected values and assertions; leave unavailable, unpromised metadata absent. Credit host-checker results only for the observed logs, spans and fields. They do not automatically prove metrics Resource, fully absent/default identity, percent-encoding, headers or maturity. Audit plans these checks without running them. CONFIG-READER separately checks reader precedence and selected Go detector collisions. An initialization-only probe does not prove a normal launch, and a launch result alone does not prove detector precedence.
Insufficient evidence: A Resource helper alone, or a parent environment change that the real launcher overrides.

[OPERATION-COVERAGE] Rule: Tie each selected source operation, list member and promised outcome to the test that checks it.
Example: A readiness-request metric cannot be assigned to a different business operation merely because both requests ran in one trial.
Evidence: Scope and required checks: Match each selected source operation, list member and promised outcome to its assertions, parameters, outputs, lifecycle phase and test scenario. A shared test or global scan is valid only when its capture scope and evidence for every selected operation and phase are explicit. Saying 'all captured records', or matching a name, is insufficient. Identify the selected application, framework and server producers from their implementation, public API, artifacts, or permitted bytecode with inspected symbols. For an unresolved producer, event or API, state its owner and the next source inspection or probe that would distinguish the possibilities; SDK mapper metadata alone does not identify a producer. Suggested work priority is not a required tool-call order. Judge producer-inventory gaps and observations bound to the wrong operation here. This item owns selectors that let a different operation satisfy the control, including method/status-only metric predicates. Judge a wholly omitted promised operation or member under CLAIM-COMPLETENESS; those require distinct evidence rather than an automatic cascade.
Insufficient evidence: A name match or unrelated observation that is not bound to the selected producer, operation and phase.

[FINDING-CLOSURE] Rule: For each finding that can be selected on its own, make sure everything its checks depend on is part of that finding or its declared dependencies.
Example: If a logging finding needs a span created only by another finding, its dependency or coupled scope must make that span available.
Evidence: Scope and required checks: For each finding that can be selected independently, trace the actual changes and producers its assertions need through their owners and all prerequisites, including required trace or metric producers. A repair owned only by a dependent or unselected finding is not available to close this finding. Attach privacy evidence to the logging finding that owns it, rather than borrowing another finding's pass. The finding that owns the complete request-to-worker-to-log path must include that integration. Group coupled repairs when they cannot deliver an independently testable result, preserving requirements and avoiding dependency cycles. Correct IDs and dependency lists alone do not prove that a finding is complete.
Insufficient evidence: Correct dependency IDs alone when the independently selectable finding still cannot deliver its promised result.

[PROPAGATION-COMPONENTS] Rule: When several propagators are selected or configured together, test each promised one through the application's real setup.
Example: A TraceContext test does not prove a separately selected baggage component. Test that component without copying baggage into logs.
Evidence: Scope and required checks: For selected or configured composite propagation, test each promised active component, carrier direction and metadata field through the actual initialization. If an application-owned guard disables the SDK, show that the required propagation setup remains reachable and carrier extraction still works on that disabled path. Provider registration or TraceContext-only evidence does not prove another component. Propagation does not authorize copying baggage into logs. Preserve the actual configuration owner's precedence, and distinguish unchanged environment text from the policy enforced by a programmatic override.
Insufficient evidence: Provider registration or TraceContext-only evidence used to claim another propagation component.

[EXPECTED-MANIFEST] Rule: Check that every declared control points at the right run, operation, lifecycle phase and typed expected result, and that its assertion can actually be checked where it is placed.
Example: A POST failure and a GET success can share a span name. Match method and outcome so one cannot satisfy the other's control.
Evidence: HTTP controls must select method AND outcome together; a shared span name or trial does not identify an operation. Grouped controls and reused evidence need explicit support for each declared operation, phase and fact. Audit plans these bindings and capture/import boundaries without inventing an observation ledger or claiming execution. This item checks missing fields or incorrect bindings in controls that are present. CLAIM-COMPLETENESS checks wholly missing promised controls or branches; do not automatically fail both for one omitted member.
Insufficient evidence: A shared span name or trial without the control's operation, phase and typed expected result.

[BAKED-EVIDENCE] Rule: When the packaged tool can represent the instrumentation or verification evidence, actually run evidence-bake with an explicit manifest and a ledger tied to the source.
Example: Writing a schema-valid evidence file by hand does not show that the packaged baker or its final validation ran.
Evidence: Scope and required checks: When instrumentation or verification evidence can be represented by the packaged tool, actually run evidence-bake with an explicit manifest and a source-bound JSON/JSONL ledger of captured or verified imported observations. Retain the generated JSON and Markdown. A future instruction, handwritten combination or schema-valid file is not enough. Verified source_import evidence may reuse established ownership without a new token. Inspect how captures or imports are interpreted and where the raw evidence is located: the tool checks ownership, types and hashes, not whether an adapter tells the truth. If evidence cannot be represented, state the exact limitation and reconcile it adequately against its own source; do not claim a tool pass. Required completed work needs a receipt bound to the final report, a retained successful packaged-validation result, and proof of the actual invocation. Missing, failed or unresolved required validation remains incomplete even when honestly disclosed. Read the trusted validation result without recalculating its mechanical checks. Only explicit current runner context makes runner validation facts authoritative; filenames or agent claims do not. Ordinary pytest does not waive this gate, and a no-execution N_A does not satisfy it. This item checks bake/validation invocation and receipt provenance; EXECUTED-COMPLETION checks actual task execution. Missing both may leave both predicates not_proven, with separate explanations rather than automatic failures elsewhere.
Insufficient evidence: A schema-valid or handwritten report without the required actual bake, final receipt and packaged-validation invocation, or treating a partial output left by a failed evidence-bake invocation as a completed bake or receipt.

[CLAIM-COMPLETENESS] Rule: Check that every selected promise in the final requirements or report, including each required member of a group, appears in the manifest and the direct-report index.
Example: If the report promises an error-path check but the manifest never lists it, a passing manifest does not prove complete coverage.
Evidence: The baker or index checker cannot detect a branch that was never declared. Audit must allocate executable checks but does not need an execution index or receipt. A genuine not-run or prerequisite-only report needs concrete reasons and must not invent observations. This item checks wholly missing promises or grouped members. Judge whether a present assertion can detect failure in that assertion's own topic, and judge its declared binding under EXPECTED-MANIFEST. Inspection, saved readback and operation binding need their own distinct evidence. Do not turn one missing promise into automatic failures of those items; mechanical consistency is also a separate deterministic gate.
Insufficient evidence: A passing declared index that omits a promise from the actual final requirements.

[LOG-OWNERSHIP] Rule: Identify the actual native logger, SDK or agent, provider and bridge, and show how startup activates them.
Example: Attaching a root bridge can change a framework logger whose original sink was initialized lazily. Check that real producer route.
Evidence: Each record needs one supported collection owner, with the original sinks preserved. Initialize each selected application, framework or server logging route through its supported public configuration or startup mechanism. Preserve its level, format, record count and opt-outs. Creating a sibling logger, finding an eligible ancestor handler, attaching a producer filter or calling a private lazy initializer does not by itself prove that the producer's native sink was initialized. Environment settings alone do not prove a working pipeline.
Insufficient evidence: Environment variables, a sibling logger or a private lazy initializer without proof of the actual native route.

[RECORD-SEMANTICS] Rule: Preserve the actual WARN/severity mapping, distinguish the source event time from observation time, and retain a useful bounded Body and supported structured values.
Example: If a bridge already supplies SeverityText, a permitted fallback name must not replace that text.
Evidence: Use the SeverityText spelling and casing supplied by the actual source or bridge; numeric severity ranges do not specify casing. An allowed short name can fill missing text, but must not replace text already supplied. Do not require EventName, exception payloads or capabilities the source does not support. log.record.original is permitted when the original is string-like AND differs from Body; do not reverse that conditional rule into a prohibition it does not state.
Insufficient evidence: Inferring text casing from numeric severity or inventing record fields that the selected source does not support.

[EXACT-SPAN-JOINS] Rule: Plan or prove that each log's TraceId and SpanId both match the exact real SDK span it belongs to, including that span's parent chain and Resource identity.
Example: Two concurrent requests can share a TraceId. The log's SpanId and ancestry must still identify the correct request's span.
Evidence: Scope and required checks: Plan or prove that each log's canonical TraceId AND SpanId match the exact real SDK span, its parent chain and source-supported Resource identity. Derive the expected SpanId from the context actually used by the bridge or API, including supported context captured by the caller. Ordinary attributes, shared or nonempty trace IDs, and correlation visible only in stdout are insufficient. A real framework INTERNAL child span is valid when it belongs to the correct request; do not require every log to reference a SERVER span, remove legitimate layer spans, copy IDs manually or force sampling. A positive workflow on a supported stack still needs its real end-to-end join. Check actual peer carriers and propagator support. If a valid carrier is unsupported, retain the dependency conformance gap; do not claim a successful join, strip its flags or raise the project's runtime requirement to hide it.
Insufficient evidence: Nonempty IDs, matching TraceId alone, manually copied IDs or stdout correlation without the exact real SDK span join.

[ASYNC-CONTEXT] Rule: Test the application's actual executor, goroutine or callback path and the concurrent left/right request pairing.
Example: A worker may inherit the right request once but retain it for the next task. A selected reuse check must exercise that same worker again.
Evidence: Separate synchronous and asynchronous probes do not prove that a worker's real log joins its SDK span. A selected reuse test must reuse the same execution unit for distinct work-item contexts and for context-free work. A selected missing-transfer negative test needs independently observed, valid caller SDK context at scheduling in both cases. Use the same path and change only context transfer, with correct detach/restore behavior. Scheduling after scope exit or logging outside any context is a different test. Limit cancellation and error checks to existing application behavior or clearly labeled supported probes. Do not invent business cancellation or treat ending a span as cancelling work.
Insufficient evidence: Separate sync/async probes, a different worker, or a missing-transfer test scheduled outside valid caller context.

[UNSAMPLED-OUTSIDE] Rule: Tell three cases apart: a valid unsampled context, logging that is genuinely outside any context, and broken wiring.
Example: A valid unsampled context may produce a correlated log without exporting a span. Compare its IDs with the SDK context actually used.
Evidence: Startup must not retain stale request IDs; do not fabricate spans or force sampling. For exact unsampled claims, compare canonical IDs and flags with independently observed SDK context actually chosen by the logging API for that record and observation boundary, including explicit context or caller capture. Later export-worker context, agreement between two logs, or a nonempty SpanId is insufficient. Do not require unsampled spans to be exported or require extra identifier fields in production logs. Audit must choose a supported observation and proof mode. A focused probe cannot close a promised full-runtime exact-value check.
Insufficient evidence: Two agreeing logs, a nonempty SpanId or later worker ambient context without the independent context observation.

[PRIVACY-BOUNDARY] Rule: Do not add raw request IDs or unbounded errors.
Example: Redacting the exported SDK record does not protect a secret already printed by the native console before that processor ran.
Evidence: Apply the selected source or operator privacy policy to every record captured by the chosen bridge, including real handled and escaping framework errors. Trace the producer and call site through its native event, supported hook or action, later renderers, and native/SDK outputs. At the claimed boundary, prove that forbidden test values are absent and check every forbidden value class in the selected policy, such as raw exception messages, rendered stacks or source paths, including failures without injected sentinels. A present assertion that cannot detect its promised failure is judged under ADDRESSABLE-ORACLES; judge an omitted forbidden class in the claimed privacy boundary here, without automatically failing both items. Distinguish registering or enqueueing a callback from invoking or completing it; do not claim an earlier lifecycle boundary than the evidence shows. Captured framework violations are part of the approved logging baseline, including direct instrumentation. During instrumentation, repair them with supported logging-only sanitization without demanding a new business audit, and preserve existing IDs and exclusions. If no supported hook exists, retain the precise gap and its owner. Suppressing every message is not redaction. Rejection and an unhandled failure at the same endpoint may have different producers and hooks.
Insufficient evidence: Redacting only a later copy after the selected native output has already exposed the forbidden value, or defining a sentinel-only privacy boundary when the selected policy forbids a whole class of values.

[PERMITTED-FIELDS] Rule: A selected privacy fix must keep the allowed diagnostic categories, effective log levels, native outputs and application behavior, in both the rendered native output and the SDK/wire output.
Example: Replacing an entire error message with a safe label can remove its useful status or category even though the sensitive value disappears.
Evidence: Before extracting bounded values, inspect the actual producer's formatting, decorations, typed fields and template arguments. Do not lose the method or status on non-success records, or prove preservation by checking only an extra safe substring. Preserve the fixed Body/category and existing formatting policy. Bounded left/right categories are allowed, and an ordinary native message does not need an extra instrumentation-only exception event. Assert the useful fields required for each selected operation. Do not invent attributes, capture payloads or headers, or impose bans broader than the operator's policy.
Insufficient evidence: A safe substring or redaction label that hides the loss of required native/exported diagnostic fields.

[LIMIT-READER] Rule: Identify the effective log attribute count/value limits, or supported unlimited behavior, for the selected path.
Example: A span attribute-limit setting does not establish the effective limits on log records.
Evidence: Follow defaults, fallbacks and programmatic precedence from startup through the provider and bridge. Public options or processors alone do not prove that values reach that path or bypass it. Inspect normalization and diagnostic helpers when a selected limit, value shape, source-backed risk or exact capability claim depends on them, even before installation. A precise versioned default or honest unverified result for an unselected SDK duty does not require that helper inventory. Span limits do not configure log limits. Body/privacy rules and Resource exemptions are separate. For unchanged SDK-owned defaults, a precise versioned explanation of ownership, or an honest unsupported/unverified result, can be sufficient; do not require tests for unused settings or claim unexecuted runtime proof.
Insufficient evidence: Public options or span limits without tracing the selected log-limit reader and enforcement path.

[LIMIT-VALUES] Rule: For selected limits, test each kind of value the limit treats differently, and check the actual number of dropped or evicted attributes.
Example: A sanitizer can preserve visible attributes but erase the SDK container's existing dropped count. Check the downstream count as well as the values.
Evidence: Include only value shapes reachable through the selected producer or sanitizer, supplied operator inputs, or an exact capability claim. For those selected limits and value shapes, distinguish strings/characters from byte arrays, recursive limits inside arrays/maps from top-level attribute count, supported depth/replacement behavior, and actual discarded or evicted attribute counts. Plan or test values below, at and above the selected limit through the promised native bridge where applicable. Direct SDK emission does not prove the native-bridge path. Preserve bridge-added attributes and each selected span or event's own SDK attribute-limit container and existing dropped counts. A parent span's count or successful truncation does not prove an event's accounting. State unsupported or Development-status shapes explicitly; do not replace or upgrade the SDK to hide them.
Insufficient evidence: Direct SDK emission in place of a promised native bridge, or a parent count used to claim an event's dropped-count preservation.

[LIMIT-DIAGNOSTICS] Rule: When checking limit diagnostics, first show that a limit actually truncated, discarded or replaced record data.
Example: A warning about invalid configuration is not evidence that a record was truncated by an attribute limit.
Evidence: An invalid-key message, uniqueness message or configuration warning with unchanged data does not automatically qualify. Preserve the source requirements: common diagnostics MAY occur; diagnostics for an affected record MUST occur at most once; Logs SDK discard diagnostics have a separate SHOULD. Follow helper calls through state changes, aggregation and the final once-only guards. Distinguish source evidence that a message can or cannot be emitted, executed diagnostic counts, and visibility at the configured sink. Report incorrect source-resolvable absence claims and upstream limitations honestly.
Insufficient evidence: An unrelated warning or source-only guard used to claim runtime diagnostic cadence or sink visibility.

[CONSTRUCTION-COST] Rule: If selected log construction is actually expensive, use a supported enablement check and prove that disabling, filtering or opting out avoids that work on the relevant path.
Example: If constructing an expensive log field is selected, a disabled-level test should show that construction was skipped; a cheap fixed message needs no artificial guard.
Evidence: Cheap fixed messages do not need artificial guards. An unverified SDK default cannot prove a required cost, privacy or operator-limit guarantee. Do not add arbitrary Body limits, invented capture paths, duplicate providers, blanket suppression or forced upgrades.
Insufficient evidence: An unverified SDK default used to close a selected cost, privacy or operator-limit requirement.

[DELIVERY-STATES] Rule: Keep each stage of a log's delivery separate, from the native log call to the final outcome, and attribute each stage to its actual owner.
Example: A receiver's copy of a log proves receipt. Without the relevant response/client evidence, acknowledgement or acceptance may still be unknown.
Evidence: Scope and required checks: Keep native log calls, enqueueing, export attempts, received copies, acknowledgement, acceptance, rejection, drops, unknown outcomes and persistence distinct under their actual batch, exporter and lifecycle owners. Derive each signal/phase's saved status, visibility and direct-assertion flag from its own raw records, response and final client outcome. An expected log-fault test may receive zero logs without proving log otlp_accepted. A healthy or recovered branch cannot supply another outcome's visibility. Preserve existing weaker or unknown states and counts without inventing enums. Client success, a decoded acknowledgement and independently observed persistence are different facts. Unknown acceptance or no observed acknowledgement cannot justify unqualified log otlp_accepted. A client operation that ended with a known error is still completed.
Insufficient evidence: Receiver arrival, client success or a healthy recovery branch used to claim a different outcome's acceptance or persistence.

[OTLP-ACK] Rule: If classifying OTLP responses is selected or claimed, decode the records in each request and link that batch or attempt to its final client outcome.
Example: With a selected partial-success response rejecting one of three records, account for two accepted and one rejected, and check that this response is not retried.
Evidence: Scope and required checks: If response classification is selected or claimed, decode the N records in each request and bind that batch/attempt to its final client outcome. A conforming HTTP 200 ExportLogsServiceResponse with no partial_success acknowledges N accepted and zero rejected. With rejected count R, it acknowledges N-R accepted and R rejected. A populated warning-only response with R=0 acknowledges N accepted and zero rejected. Populated partial-success or warning responses MUST NOT be retried. An invalid or unrelated HTTP 200 body, or SDK success alone, proves neither correct decoding nor acceptance. Account for every received request and final outcome. Keep unresolved negative-count or size-related acceptance unknown. Ordinary OTLP export alone does not require a protocol-conformance suite.
Insufficient evidence: HTTP 200 or SDK success without the selected response decoding, per-request accounting and terminal client outcome.

[RETRY-CLASSIFICATION] Rule: For selected retry tests, use actual client and receiver evidence to distinguish completed negative responses from stalls, with counts and raw-evidence links for each outcome.
Example: Zero retries on a rejected request is inconclusive when retries were disabled for every request, including the positive control.
Evidence: To prove a no-retry result, use a policy that can retry and a positive control that actually retries; disabled or exhausted retries cannot prove it. HTTP 429/502/503/504 SHOULD retry; other 4xx/5xx responses MUST NOT. Preserve operator policy and the selected standard's transient-error exponential backoff, jitter, transport-specific Retry-After or RetryInfo, and remaining-budget conditions. Server intent, null counts or total elapsed time alone do not establish the client outcome. Do not add an application retry loop merely to expose SDK internals.
Insufficient evidence: Zero retries when retries were disabled/exhausted, or server intent without the client outcome.

[DEADLINE-BUDGET] Rule: For selected exact deadlines, follow the budget from creation through propagation, retries, waits and final use.
Example: A one-second whole-export budget cannot become a new one-second budget for each retry. The value is illustrative; use the selected budget.
Evidence: Retain units, effective defaults and fallbacks, and measure any overshoot. Distinguish a configured timeout, per-attempt timeout, whole-export budget and earlier caller cancellation. A standard export budget includes every attempt and wait; it cannot restart for each request. A throttle longer than the remaining budget must not cause an early retry. Checking elapsed time only after failure, measuring process or shutdown duration, or assigning a timeout value does not prove a strict batch deadline. Preserve required processor Export synchronization without adding duplicate application locks or confusing it with concurrent exporter requests.
Insufficient evidence: An assigned timeout or total process/shutdown duration used to prove a strict whole-export budget.

[PENDING-DRAIN] Rule: To prove selected shutdown draining, identify a genuinely queued or pending record when provider draining starts.
Example: Finding a final log in a query after process exit does not show that it arrived before the SDK child exited.
Evidence: Use the normal launcher and configured application stop path, and establish the effective queue, schedule and batch conditions. A record logged before stopping may already have exported; holding a receiver response may prove only an in-flight export. Show that this exact record was decoded before the actual SDK child exited, using receiver observation with child liveness or an awaited receipt→conforming acknowledgement→shutdown sequence. ObservedTimestamp may be the SDK emission time, not receiver ingestion order. After-exit queries, a nil shutdown error, exit code zero or launcher wait timing alone are insufficient. This item checks pending state and receipt-before-exit order; FINAL-RECORD checks final-record fields and record counts.
Insufficient evidence: A final log found only after exit, an exit code of zero, or a held response that proves only in-flight export.

[FINAL-RECORD] Rule: Check the selected final log record from the real stop cycle, within its phase and observation window.
Example: A total of two records can hide a missing final record plus a duplicate earlier record. Check each required record's identity and count.
Evidence: Scope and required checks: Check the selected final record from the actual stop cycle, phase and observation window: counts for each body/identity, Body, severity, expected Resource, and both context IDs or their required absence. A total count can hide one missing record and one duplicate. Healthy joins, focused export tests, opt-out tests, live snapshots or cleanup cannot replace this proof. Reuse real application logs where possible; do not add a production log solely for testing or tune settings arbitrarily. Required instrumentation drain checks that can safely run must run unless genuinely blocked. Retain shutdown errors and respect the actual child lifetime when describing the result. This item checks final-record content and multiplicity; PENDING-DRAIN checks queue state and receipt-before-exit order.
Insufficient evidence: An aggregate count or another successful probe instead of the stop cycle's actual final record and multiplicity.

[REPEATED-STOP] Rule: For selected stop tests, state which stop request is sent and to which process, how it reaches the application's handler or finalizer from the launcher, what should happen, and the time budget and event order the source supports.
Example: If application policy promises uninterrupted drain, send the selected second signal while drain is active and check that it does not start another finalizer.
Evidence: Check handler registration, removal and default fallback after the first request. Send the selected same or different second signal to that same process while final logging or provider draining is active. Do not reset the budget, and retain the second request's outcome. If application policy requires uninterrupted draining, prove no interruption and exactly one finalization, without default termination or a second finalizer. If policy permits forced termination on repetition, record that distinct result; it does not prove graceful draining or final receipt. The fixture README's Graceful-stop policy is application policy, not a universal OpenTelemetry signal rule.
Insufficient evidence: A second signal sent outside active finalization, or forced termination presented as graceful drain.

[LATE-CALLBACK] Rule: For a selected claim that a late callback is suppressed, bounded or handled safely, follow that callback from registration to its final effect.
Example: A detached callback may still be invoked from an existing reference. An idempotent closed owner can make that invocation harmless.
Evidence: Scope and required checks: For a selected claim about suppressing, bounding or safely handling a late callback, follow dispatch and cleanup registrations, retained references, the actual closed state, callback invocation and its final effect. Removing a callback from dispatch is not the same as cancelling it. Invocation, completed teardown, cancellation and harmless repeated execution are different facts. If source shows that an already-closed owner safely ignores a repeated callback, prove that required effect and budget. Do not require callback removal, manipulate unsupported registries, or claim a runtime hang merely because invocation is possible.
Insufficient evidence: Assuming dispatch removal cancelled an already retained callback, or assuming possible invocation proves a hang.

[RETRY-LINEAGE] Rule: For a selected retry test, identify the batch, the retry decision and the final outcome.
Example: A healthy later batch does not prove that an earlier failed batch recovered. Match the retried request to that original batch.
Evidence: Scope and required checks: A selected retry test must identify a source-supported retryable response or connection event, the actual batch/trial, SDK retry policy and wait implementation, remaining budget, measured waits and final outcome. Distinguish recovery of the failed batch from later healthy batches and from persistent exhaustion or deadline termination. Existing SDK backoff and jitter may be sufficient; server throttling is not always required. Use request fingerprints, timestamps and bound client outcomes to show which attempts belong together. Different decoded record sets, a generic failure/stall label, server intent or another export's deadline do not establish that relationship. Leave unmatched client outcomes unknown instead of assigning acceptance.
Insufficient evidence: A later healthy batch, generic fault label or unrelated deadline used as proof that the failed batch retried or recovered.

[APP-FAULT-PATH] Rule: Audit must plan a feasible, isolated way to exercise the selected fault.
Example: A direct exporter unit test can reveal an SDK failure but does not show what happens through the application bootstrap, bridge and real operation.
Evidence: Execution claims must use actual application initialization, the production provider/processor path including selected batching, the bridge and real operations. A transport or exporter seam limited to one instance can prove app_test; an SDK-only substitute cannot prove that complete application path. Preserve production guards and shared receivers. Do not intercept or redirect transport globally. Keep selected independent controls for direct export, processors, cancellation and persistent failure, but do not invent a matrix of unselected faults or a new business feature. Distinguish normal-launch proof from focused application tests. This item checks the actual fault path and preservation of the selected safe seam, including selected Node failure responses and healthy other-signal receipts there. It does not add unselected live-fault ordering or independent-signal requirements; explicitly selected requirements remain in their own criteria.
Insufficient evidence: An SDK-only substitute or global transport redirection used to claim the selected safe application fault boundary.

[DIAGNOSTIC-OBSERVATION] Rule: When claiming a diagnostic count or absence, trace the actual emitting operation through its callers or aggregate route, logger/handler and configured sink.
Example: A zero diagnostic count is inconclusive if the test never showed that its actual matcher and configured sink can observe that diagnostic.
Evidence: Internal SDK logging and the public error handler may take different routes. Replacing the handler with a counter does not prove the original native route. Validate the actual source-supported match rule with a retained positive case where the message is emitted, raw matching evidence and an observation window. Source calls or once-only guards do not prove runtime visibility. Configured suppression or source-confirmed non-emission can explain zero; do not add production diagnostics merely to obtain a count. One helper without warnings or one handler setup cannot prove absence for every operation. An enabled but untested pipeline is not 'not configured'.
Insufficient evidence: A replacement counting handler, uncalibrated matcher or source call alone used to claim original-sink visibility.

[FAULT-CLEANUP] Rule: Finish cleanup of test-owned work before retrying or finalizing evidence. Keep observing diagnostics until the selected work reaches its final client and diagnostic outcome.
Example: If a caller times out while a test receiver thread is still stalled, releasing the caller does not prove that the receiver work or its later diagnostics ended.
Evidence: After a caller timeout, release or clean up test-owned work before restoring handlers or sinks. A finished wait does not mean the work finished. If capture stops first, leave later effects unknown and complete bounded cleanup of owned work, without attributing it to the next trial. Late completion or varying payloads must not produce a false zero-count or upper-bound pass. Check that saved summaries agree with the validated raw match rules, actual observation windows, and cleanup/restoration order.
For test-owned application probes, include failed setup and earlier retries in the cleanup obligation. Audit plans this check; instrumentation and verification retain the actual ownership and cleanup evidence. A launcher exit or a signal sent to one process found by name does not prove its children stopped. Stop the owned process group or platform equivalent, confirm its members exited, and retain capture through writer exit and EOF within the cleanup budget before retrying or finalizing evidence. If members or writers remain after escalation and the cleanup deadline, retain the failure and unknown later effects and stop dependent trials; do not wait indefinitely or claim cleanup succeeded. Preserve raw logs and cleanup failures without signaling user-owned processes.
Insufficient evidence: A launcher exit or name-matched signal used to claim that owned probe children stopped; Stopping capture when the caller times out while the underlying work and its possible diagnostics remain active.

[LIVE-FAULT-ORDER] Rule: A claim that the application keeps working after a log failure needs the right event order.
Example: A request that finishes before the logging client sees the fault cannot prove that application work continued after the fault.
Evidence: Either the originating SDK/client observes the selected failure or refusal before the later application/native work, or the log operation is explicitly still blocked while that work progresses. Audit plans this sequence; execution must retain the actual events while the application and producers are alive. Receiver arrival or response status alone does not prove the client observed it. A fault first exercised during shutdown does not prove live failure isolation. Keep long batch schedules used for pending-drain tests separate. Unexecuted fault cases remain unproven.
Insufficient evidence: Receiver arrival or a shutdown-only fault used to claim the client observed a live failure before later work.

[INDEPENDENT-SIGNALS] Rule: For selected log-fault isolation, decode the received output that proves progress of each other configured signal, such as traces or metrics.
Example: A metric from a readiness request cannot prove that the selected business request still emitted metrics during the log fault.
Evidence: Bind those receipts to the selected originating operations after the observed client failure or during the selected blocked interval. A signal endpoint, timestamp or byte count alone is insufficient. Use actual producer-owned receipts. Unrelated healthy work and traffic sent before the fault cannot prove the required continued operation.
Insufficient evidence: Before-fault traffic, unrelated healthy operations, endpoint names or byte counts without decoded attributable signal output.

[APP-COMPATIBILITY] Rule: Preserve application routes and behavior, legitimate layer spans, native log sinks, and supported runtimes and consumers.
Example: A local logging change must not silently replace the operator's existing trace destination or increase the project's runtime requirement.
Evidence: Keep added local logs local and preserve existing trace and metric behavior. Do not add unrequested cloud configuration, SDK upgrades, unrelated business instrumentation or a higher runtime requirement. Repair approved logging-baseline failures while retaining explicit exclusions and user-owned configuration.
Insufficient evidence: A logging repair that changes unrelated application behavior, operator configuration or supported runtimes.

[SOURCE-CLAUSES] Rule: For each claim in scope, record where its rule comes from, how strong it is, and what was actually proved.
Example: A generic specification link cannot substantiate a claim about one exact revision and operation that the agent did not inspect.
Evidence: Scope and required checks: For selected application/operator behavior, changed configuration, source-supported risks and actual capability claims, retain the primary source, version/date, applicable conditions, requirement strength, owner or disposition, and proof boundary. An exact standards-conformance or revision claim needs the primary text actually inspected, including the relevant section or operation. A remembered revision, generic link, unrelated excerpt or SDK comment is insufficient. Unchanged requirements may be referenced through bounded excerpts or exact immutable evidence rows. A compact versioned explanation can document a source-known default. Do not invent a precise revision when only the URL and date are known. Bare workflow tasks do not need to repeat an exhaustive PR-wide inventory of standards clauses.
Insufficient evidence: A remembered revision, generic URL or unrelated source range used to support an exact standards claim.

[DUTY-OWNERS] Rule: Assign each selected responsibility to its actual owner: SDK, bridge, instrumentation or semantic-convention author, application, receiver or operator.
Example: If the SDK already provides a required behavior, use that supported guarantee instead of requiring a duplicate application implementation.
Evidence: An SDK guarantee already supported on the selected path needs no duplicate application implementation. Unchanged, unselected responsibilities elsewhere do not need a per-service clause inventory or exhaustive certification. State accurate source/default, unsupported or unverified conditions and the next steps needed to resolve gaps. Refresh capability findings after installation or probes. An external or delegated limitation cannot close a selected critical application requirement or remove an earlier promise after the fact. Do not tune arbitrarily, require one framework recipe, or rewrite/upgrade an SDK merely to hide an upstream limitation.
Insufficient evidence: An external limitation used to close a critical application promise or remove it after the fact.

[TRANSPORT-BOUNDS] Rule: Only require message-size or decompression tests when the application's own code sets the limit or we change it, the operator supplied a policy, the source shows a risk, or the work makes an exact capability or conformance claim.
Example: A client test that rejects a large response does not establish how the external receiver limits incoming requests.
Evidence: Scope and required checks: Require transport-size or decompression tests only for an application-owned or changed limit, supplied operator policy, source-supported risk, or exact capability/conformance claim. Ordinary SDK-owned HTTP export, endpoint/timeout setup, or a disclosed status/body limitation does not select other transport responsibilities. Apply only the selected surface and its HTTP or corresponding gRPC rules. The recommended 64 MiB request and 4 MiB response sizes are not mandatory application tuning; making limits configurable remains SHOULD. Receiver request limit: retain bounding/decompression MUST and HTTP 413 on overflow. Exporter request limit: retain pre-compression bounding SHOULD, MUST NOT send above an active limit, and discard-diagnostic SHOULD. Client response limit: retain bounding/decompression MUST, non-retryable oversize MUST, and discard-diagnostic SHOULD. Receiver response limit: retain pre-compression bounding MUST; oversized partial responses SHOULD be reduced without changing meaning when possible/practical, MAY lose optional diagnostics, and MUST return HTTP 500 with acceptance unspecified if still oversized. For every selected limit, identify the actual owner/reader, test input and send, discard or response outcome. A request check, timeout or client simulation cannot certify another surface or an external receiver. State external ownership honestly. Claims about receiver implementation or conformance need evidence from that receiver; ordinary applications need not certify it.
Insufficient evidence: A test at one transport surface used to certify a different surface or an external receiver.

[EXACT-API] Rule: For a concrete fix, or an exact claim about a capability, default or absence, find the public API involved and follow it to the code that actually uses the value.
Example: Finding a constructor option does not prove the application passes it to the overload actually used at startup.
Evidence: Scope and required checks: For a concrete repair or exact capability, default or absence claim, find the declaring public symbol, selected overload, final native/container conversion and implementation that actually consumes it. Follow relevant parsing, defaults, retries and diagnostic helpers. An interface signature, documentation, another reader's special default value or an unused helper does not prove that concrete path. A source-resolvable contradiction is still a failure even if labeled Not run. A focused probe proves only what it exercised. Respect the applicability of private extensions instead of imposing unrelated standard defaults.
Insufficient evidence: A signature, another overload/reader or an unused helper used to claim the actual consuming implementation.

[NORMATIVE-DIRECTION] Rule: Check the final generated explanation of a standard against the exact source it cites: who the rule applies to, the operation, condition, required consequence and direction, strength, and qualifications.
Example: A rule saying 'when A, require B' does not also mean 'B is allowed only when A' unless the source states that converse.
Evidence: A correct source file or initial ledger does not validate a reversed implication or an unsupported converse in the final report. Keep recommendations, permissions, mandatory fallback behavior, requirements adopted by reference, and compatibility qualifications distinct. Do not turn SHOULD/MAY into an unconditional application MUST, or weaken an applicable MUST into an optional choice.
Insufficient evidence: A correct source citation attached to a reversed implication or changed requirement strength.

[ONEMIT-CONTRACT] Rule: For selected log-processor behavior, risks or conformance claims, keep three OnEmit rules separate, each at its own strength.
Example: The SDK calling a custom OnEmit callback synchronously does not prove that network I/O inside that callback is nonblocking.
Evidence: Scope and required checks: For selected processor behavior, risk or conformance claims, distinguish these requirements: the SDK runs OnEmit synchronously on the emitting thread; nonblocking and nonthrowing behavior is SHOULD; mutation visibility for a directly registered processor is MUST. An application-owned callback needs evidence about its actual work/actions and an applicable assertion, or a precise limitation. SDK guarantees or synchronous invocation alone do not prove that application code cannot block or throw. If a selected filtering processor supports or wraps Enabled, assess filtering in OnEmit independently. LoggerConfig defaults alone do not require that test. An unchanged built-in batch processor does not by itself select application OnEmit duties. Application progress during stalled export is a separate requirement; it does not select all three OnEmit clauses. A selected read-only observer needs the applicable nonblocking/nonthrowing assessment, but does not select mutation visibility unless it changes records. Unchanged, unselected SDK callbacks need no inventory or duplicate implementation.
Insufficient evidence: SDK synchrony alone used to claim that application callback work cannot block or throw.

[MATURITY] Rule: State maturity separately for the relevant data model/specification and for the actual installed or proposed SDK, bridge, component and API.
Example: A stable record data model does not establish that the installed bridge package is stable.
Evidence: Stable record semantics do not prove that a component is stable. One component's source comment cannot label the entire language beta. State when maturity is absent or has not been inspected. Refresh actual capability results after installation or probes. Do not force upgrades or treat source capability as inherited runtime success.
Insufficient evidence: Stable semantics or one component comment used to label the maturity of an entire SDK/bridge stack.

[BRIDGE-ERROR-AUTHORITY] Rule: If our change adds a global log bridge, or makes the application responsible for one, keep any existing custom or strict error handler and set up a separate error route before turning on the provider or bridge.
Example: A newly installed global bridge must not replace an existing strict error handler with a permissive counting handler merely to pass a test.
Evidence: A returned global delegator is not a snapshot of the original native handler. An existing safe route does not need replacement. Bind the proof to the actual failing operation and handler authority. When the selected initialization can emit an error or diagnostic, include that startup path: audit allocates the expected route and observation; instrumentation and verification check it through the actual initialization. A later export-failure test does not establish startup routing. Source-confirmed safe suppression is valid without forcing a diagnostic or replacing an adequate route. Generic setup or a replacement counting handler cannot prove preservation of the selected native error route.
Insufficient evidence: A global delegator or replacement counter used to claim preservation of the original error-handler authority, or a later export-failure test used to claim safe startup routing.

[NAME-SYNTAX] Rule: For selected new telemetry names, follow the standard's naming rules at their stated strength, using ecosystem evidence and compatibility.
Example: An optional log.iostream field need not be added; if it is selected, use an applicable known value before choosing a custom one.
Evidence: Scope and required checks: For selected new telemetry names, preserve the standard's valid-Unicode MUST, lowercase/dot/snake SHOULD, and established-concatenation-over-underscore SHOULD, considering ecosystem evidence and compatibility. One API or SDK symbol's spelling alone is insufficient. If optional log.iostream is used and a known value applies, use it; otherwise custom values MAY be used. Names emitted unchanged by SDK or framework instrumentation are not new application-defined names. For those names, assess selected semantic-convention version/profile and compatibility promises without requiring an application naming ledger. Naming recommendations and optional fields must not become unconditional application features.
Insufficient evidence: One API spelling used as ecosystem naming evidence, or a recommendation turned into a required optional feature.

[SEMANTIC-EVENT-DEFINITION] Rule: For a selected formal semantic-event definition in Development status, retain the rules: MUST NOT prescribe ObservedTimestamp or SeverityText, and Body is only a string display message.
Example: A restriction on a formal Development event definition does not prohibit the SDK from populating SeverityText on an ordinary log record.
Evidence: These restrictions apply to formal event definitions, not SDK-populated fields or structured Body values in ordinary logs. Do not require EventName, forbid legitimate ordinary record values, or infer stable SDK/API maturity from event-model semantics.
Insufficient evidence: Applying formal event-definition restrictions as a ban on legitimate ordinary log values.

[LOCAL-DESTINATION] Rule: For selected local-log policy, find which configuration input actually wins.
Example: A configured Studio origin can identify its OTLP base through /api/health. A loopback logs URL alone cannot identify the receiver; an audit can instead name the receiver check for the next stage.
Evidence: Scope and required checks: For selected local-log policy, find the configuration input that actually wins: programmatic options, files, loaders, environment or child-VM options. Compare its effective transport, host/port and signal path with the detected/approved receiver or explicitly authorized fixture destination. When using a configured Studio origin for HTTP status, inspect /api/health, require kind=obstudio, and compare its advertised OTLP base using the signal endpoint rules. Do not guess another status path or infer receiver identity from an arbitrary JSON response. Loopback alone does not identify the receiver. Treating the current runtime endpoint as its own approval is not independent approval. An approved signal-specific logs endpoint A must still work when an unused generic endpoint is B. Preserve approved alternate receivers and supported resolution; do not add runtime discovery, require one universal fixed port or silently override operator policy. State exact unresolved boundaries. For audit, an explicit unresolved disposition that names the receiver-approval check for instrumentation or verification satisfies the approval-planning obligation; it does not establish that the endpoint is approved. This item checks destination approval/resolution and the winning input. It also owns the attached Java launcher checks: isolate local-log conflicts from application/native/trace/metric startup, retain unresolved JVM-argument preflight blockers, and test actual conflicts and A-versus-B cases. CREDENTIAL-ISOLATION checks original header preservation and credential authority. A header-only loss is not a second destination failure.
Insufficient evidence: Approving whichever endpoint the runtime supplies, or treating every loopback alias as independently approved.

[CREDENTIAL-ISOLATION] Rule: Preserve valid signal-specific local-log headers for the official SDK to parse, without replacing them with empty headers.
Example: A conflict in generic headers may isolate the added log path, but it must not erase the operator's trace and metric credentials.
Evidence: Keep a generic-header conflict isolated to the added local-log path, preserving trace/metric settings and native output. Any required credential migration or removal belongs to operator-resolved preflight configuration. Startup must not remove generic headers or copy/rewrite them into signal-specific variables just to activate logs. For selected conflicts at the winning input, assert the actual credential handling, activation and independent signals; environment-helper checks alone are insufficient. This item owns header preservation and credential authority from its visible requirements. LOCAL-DESTINATION owns destination approval and the attached Java launcher/preflight/startup clauses; do not import unseen Java additions or fail this item again for the same startup/isolation omission. SIGNAL-ACTIVATION checks whether a selected branch invokes policy checks. No other item's verdict automatically determines this one.
Insufficient evidence: Removing generic credentials at startup or checking only an environment helper while losing real signal-specific headers.

[HTTP-ENDPOINTS] Rule: When OTLP/HTTP endpoint resolution is selected, use a signal-specific URL unchanged, including root when it has no path.
Example: A generic base /collector/v1/traces resolves logs to /collector/v1/traces/v1/logs; do not silently strip the signal-looking suffix.
Evidence: For a generic endpoint, keep the entire base path and append v1/<signal>, adding a separating slash. A suffix that looks like another signal path does not allow replacing it. Reuse the SDK's actual resolver when supported. Prove that the selected precedence and protocol cases reach the effective consumer; inspecting environment text alone is insufficient. Do not add a universal custom parser in place of checking the actual resolution path.
Insufficient evidence: Stripping a signal-looking generic base suffix or checking only environment text without effective resolution.

[COMMAND-BOUNDARY] Rule: For a selected zero-code or launcher command, treat everything after the application-command separator as application arguments.
Example: An application argument after the command separator must not be reinterpreted as an instrumentor flag that bypasses the checked local-log policy.
Evidence: Those arguments must not silently override settings already checked by local policy. Inspect the installed command parser and actual child invocation. A helper or preflight check before later option rewriting does not prove the final boundary. Preserve supported operator and application options. State unsupported combinations explicitly rather than replacing the general command parser.
Insufficient evidence: A preflight result taken before later command parsing rewrites the effective child settings.

[METRIC-SEMANTICS] Rule: For a selected stable or legacy instrumentation mode, or a metric capability claim, find the mode actually in effect and the metric names, units, fields and compatibility aliases the source supports for it.
Example: A metric name checked in legacy mode does not prove the name promised for a selected stable mode.
Evidence: Plan or prove them at the stated application boundary. A default-mode metric assertion does not prove an operator-selected or promised mode that changes those values. Unchanged modes described only from source do not require a hypothetical matrix of runtime tests. Do not invent optional metadata.
Insufficient evidence: A default-mode metric assertion presented without qualification as proof of a different selected mode.

[EXCEPTION-CAPTURE] Rule: For a selected decorator or context-manager exception requirement, inspect how the actual API records escaping exceptions and error status, including any explicit recording on that same span.
Example: If the selected context manager already records an escaping exception, explicitly recording it again on the same span can duplicate it.
Evidence: Prevent the selected duplicate records without suppressing the legitimate escaping-exception result. Distinguish an exception handled within a successful operation from an error escaping the selected context. Follow the actual API path and operator privacy policy. Do not add extra exception events or impose a universal ban on supported exception fields.
Insufficient evidence: Duplicated same-span exception recording, or suppressing the legitimate escaping outcome to avoid duplicates.
judge_inputs: Grade the current stage identified by the actor task. Report a conflicting trusted runner role as an input conflict; do not transfer evidence or credit between stages. For otel-audit, assess source-backed findings and the proposed plan. For each applicable behavior requirement, look for a planned action, an expected outcome, the evidence to retain and any unresolved boundary. Do not require installed instrumentation, application startup, runtime tests, emitted telemetry, delivery/shutdown results or runtime evidence receipts during audit. A complete applicable plan satisfies the planning obligation. Missing required audit work, including source inspection, plan allocation or saved readback, is not_proven. A plan to inspect later does not satisfy an audit item's current source-inspection obligation unless that item permits an unverified disposition and the audit records it. Grade a written plan as fail when it contradicts inspected source or would violate an applicable requirement if executed as written. Missing detail alone is not_proven. A false execution claim fails only the item whose truthfulness or provenance requirement it violates. Use not_applicable only when the entire item concerns later execution and has no applicable planning or truthfulness obligation. Factual claims about current code or SDK behavior still need the source evidence required by that item, or an unverified disposition where the item permits it. For otel-instrument and otel-verify, require the actual work and evidence within that role: a proposed test or future promise does not satisfy required execution. Being part of a paired workflow does not make audit responsible for later-stage execution, and a later-stage failure must not be copied into the audit verdict.

Inspect the actual service, audit/selection and relevant saved plans/reports. Decide whether each item applies before grading it. Audit is read-only. Only an untouched standalone verification fixture that starts without a required audit or selection may stop at the confirmed missing prerequisite. For that genuine negative test, the task ends after prerequisite inspection: later checks are not_applicable, receive no runtime credit and need no post-gate analysis. Still grade prerequisite inspection, read-only behavior and truthful reporting, including any observed violations. This exception never applies to a paired instrumented workflow.

Use source and raw evidence visible in files or tool results. Retrieve required sections cut off by tool output. Keeping a file, running a successful command or archiving output without reading it does not by itself prove a source fact. Distinguish an observed failure from missing proof. Explain legitimate not_applicable results using the actual task scope.

Instrumentation must actually execute the required work and pass the unchanged host checker. Verification with satisfied prerequisites must execute its required read-only checks. The paired runner also reruns the unchanged checker independently after instrumentation and verification; an agent's success claim is not an independent receipt. Credit runner results only when explicit current runner context identifies the actual checks and exact current proof paths. A filename or run-* prefix does not establish runner authority; without that context, treat the file as agent-produced evidence. Ordinary pytest does not waive the required instrumentation checker. Missing required proof remains not_proven and earns no runtime credit. Credit host artifacts only for the boundary they actually observe.

Use supplied runner validation facts only when explicit current runner context binds them to an actual executed check. Read the bound receipt and retained packaged-validation result; do not recalculate mechanical hashes, schema checks or index consistency. A file named evidence-receipt-check.json is not independent authority by itself. In ordinary pytest, inspect proof that packaged validation was actually invoked, or leave the required gate not_proven. For instrumentation and verification that require execution, honest disclosure and a validated no-execution N_A do not satisfy required completed execution. Audit is assessed on its applicable planning and source-evidence obligations. BAKED-EVIDENCE checks bake/receipt provenance; CLAIM-COMPLETENESS checks promised coverage. A mechanical failure is a separate deterministic result, not an automatic failure of unrelated semantic checks. Falsely claiming a required gate completed is an observed failure of its provenance requirement; honestly reporting it unresolved is not_proven. Neither meets required execution, and neither automatically fails unrelated items.

Live host captures and later cleanup do not prove persistence after exit or draining of the final record. If either is promised, require its own evidence at the claimed boundary. A different healthy branch cannot prove it.

Grade only the predicates assigned to this group, using each item's stated scope, responsibility and requirement strength. For an item with several applicable clauses, pass requires all of them. An observed violation means fail; otherwise missing required proof means not_proven. Use not_applicable only when the entire item is outside the task, including checks after the blocker in a genuine standalone missing-prerequisite test. Judge required work at the current stage: missing required audit work (source inspection, plan allocation or saved readback) remains not_proven; missing required execution in instrumentation or verification remains not_proven even when planned, blocked or disclosed. Do not require criteria hidden from this group or another judge's verdict. A wholly missing promise belongs to CLAIM-COMPLETENESS. Inspection, saved readback and operation-binding failures need their own distinct evidence. Do not automatically copy another item's failure. Shared evidence is allowed, and genuinely different requirements retain separate results. Optional reference features do not become task requirements. Each item uses Rule, Example, Evidence and Insufficient evidence. Read all four together. Examples illustrate existing requirements; do not require their sample names, values or implementation unless the actual task/input selects them. Accept equivalent representative values and valid tests. Examples add no unselected work, and copying an example is not execution evidence. Explicit task requirements and supplied fixture values remain binding. Apply the item's role and applicability conditions to every section: audit plans required execution, while instrumentation and verification execute only within their existing authority. The Insufficient evidence examples are not exhaustive. They describe what does not by itself prove the rule. Missing proof alone is not_proven; an observed violation of an applicable requirement is fail. This includes false completion claims where the item treats them as violations. Optional or unselected work stays optional, and source-only evidence or an unsupported/unverified disposition remains valid wherever that item's rule allows it. Judge the completed allocation and reconciliation rather than draft chronology. A complete equivalent inspection need not follow a suggested tool-call order. Still enforce required preflight before mutation, skill loading before application work, and fresh checks and saved readback after the last relevant edit.
